obstrusion: Source spelling under review: no reliable dictionary meaning has been verified. It is retained for audit completeness and is excluded from flashcards and all quizzes. Do not memorize a guessed definition.
Check a reliable dictionary and the original source before studying an uncertain spelling.
adlib: The source uses the closed spelling adlib; ad-lib is the usual dictionary spelling. The intended sense is to improvise without a prepared script.
Connect ad-lib with an actor inventing a line on the spot.
forgone: Forgone is the past participle of forgo, meaning to go without. Foregone, with an extra e, belongs to forego and appears in foregone conclusion.
Forgone: something you have gone without.
albeit: Albeit is a formal conjunction meaning although. It commonly introduces a short qualifying phrase: useful, albeit expensive.
Read albeit as although or even though.
ad hoc: Ad hoc is a two-word expression for something created for one particular purpose rather than generally planned. Keep the space when spelling it.
An ad hoc committee is assembled for this one task.
protégé: A protégé is a person guided and supported by a more experienced mentor. The accented spelling is preserved from the source.
A mentor guides a protégé; keep the two accents.
risqué: Risqué describes material that is suggestive or slightly indecent. It does not simply mean dangerous or risky.
Risqué concerns suggestive content; risky concerns possible danger.
touché: Touché is an interjection acknowledging an effective reply. It comes from fencing language and is not an adjective meaning touched.
retard: Study only the verb here, meaning to delay or slow progress. The related noun used to label a person is an offensive slur and is not taught.
To retard growth is to slow growth; delay is the useful synonym.
spastic: In medical use, spastic describes involuntary muscle stiffness or spasms. Using the word as an insult about a person is offensive.
Keep this word in its medical context; use respectful language about people.
imbecility: This is a dated and derogatory word for extreme foolishness. It also has an obsolete historical medical use; it is not an appropriate label for a person with a disability.
Recognize the word in older writing; choose neutral descriptions in your own speech.
crone: Crone is a derogatory or storybook term for an old woman. The age and insulting tone are part of its meaning.
Recognize the fairy-tale term without applying it to real people.
effeminacy: Effeminacy describes traits traditionally stereotyped as feminine in a man. It is often disapproving or dated and reflects a social judgment, not a defect.
Notice the writer’s attitude and gender stereotype rather than adopting it.
shrewish: Shrewish means bad-tempered or nagging and has traditionally been applied to women. It can carry a dated, sexist tone.
Recognize its critical tone; prefer precise descriptions of behavior.
simpleton: Simpleton is an insulting term for a person thought foolish or easily deceived. It is useful to recognize in fiction, not to use as a label for classmates.
The ending names a person; the tone is contemptuous.
uncivilized: Here uncivilized describes cruel or impolite behavior. Applying the word to entire cultures can express prejudice and should be avoided.
Judge the specific behavior described in the sentence.
ejaculate: This lesson uses the literary sense to exclaim suddenly. The word also has a biological meaning, so context is essential.
In older dialogue, an abrupt exclamation can be described with this verb.
homely: In American English homely can mean plain or unattractive in appearance; in British English it can mean comfortable and welcoming. This lesson uses the American appearance sense.
Check the setting: a plain-looking face or a cozy home.
cahier: Cahier is a rare borrowed word for a notebook; in French history it can refer to a written list of grievances. It is not cashier.
Picture a notebook, not a shop’s cash desk.
pipkin: A pipkin is a small earthenware cooking pot, a historical household term. It does not mean a seed or a small pumpkin.
Picture a little clay pot beside the hearth.
sectile: Sectile is a technical adjective for a material that can be cut smoothly into thin slices. It differs from brittle, which breaks or crumbles.
scatheless: Scatheless is a rare literary word meaning unharmed or uninjured, like unscathed. Its rarity does not make it a source error.
Link scatheless with unscathed: no harm done.
alate: Alate is a biological adjective meaning winged. It often distinguishes a winged insect form from a wingless one.
Imagine the wings of a flying ant.
apterous: Apterous means wingless and is used especially in descriptions of insects. It contrasts with alate.
Compare apterous without wings and alate with wings.
cinerary: Cinerary relates to ashes, especially the ashes of a cremated person. It is not culinary, which relates to cooking.
A cinerary urn holds ashes; a culinary tool belongs in a kitchen.
imbrue: Imbrue is a literary verb meaning to stain or soak, especially with blood. It is different from imbue, meaning to fill with a quality.
Imbrue stains; imbue fills with an influence or feeling.
nepenthe: Nepenthe is a literary or mythological substance believed to remove sorrow. It is not a modern treatment recommendation.
Picture a mythical drink of forgetfulness in an old poem.
superable: Superable means able to be overcome. It is much rarer than its opposite, insuperable.
vincible: Vincible means capable of being defeated. The more familiar invincible means impossible to defeat.
Remove in- from invincible to reverse the meaning.
titian: Titian describes reddish-gold or auburn hair. The color term derives from the painter Titian and may also be capitalized.
Picture warm reddish-gold hair in a portrait.
straight-laced: Straight-laced means strict or conventional about behavior. Strait-laced is another established spelling; this bank preserves the source form.
Picture someone insisting on every traditional rule.
heteronyms: Heteronyms share a spelling but differ in pronunciation and meaning, such as lead the metal and lead meaning guide.
Same written form, different spoken forms and senses.
confer: This lesson uses confer meaning consult or discuss. Confer can also mean grant, as in confer an award; use the sentence to select the sense.
Confer with a colleague; confer a prize on a winner.
engage: This lesson uses engage meaning hire or obtain the services of someone. Other senses include attract attention and take part.
Engage a guide means hire a guide.
gloss: Here gloss is a shiny surface or luster. As a different noun, a gloss can be a short explanation of a word.
A polished surface has gloss; a glossary explains terms.
cast: This lesson uses cast as a verb meaning throw. The same spelling can name the actors in a play or a rigid support for an injured limb.
Cast a line into the water: send or throw it out.
disguise: This lesson uses disguise as a noun for an appearance that hides identity. The same spelling can also be a verb.
A costume can be a disguise; to disguise is to hide identity.
sweep: This lesson uses the everyday verb meaning clean with a brush. In other contexts it can mean move broadly or win every contest in a series.
Picture a broom gathering crumbs into a pile.
torturous: Torturous means causing severe suffering. Tortuous means winding, complicated, or indirect; the extra r changes the meaning.
Torturous pain hurts; a tortuous path twists.
veracious: Veracious means truthful. Voracious means extremely eager to eat, read, or consume.
Veracious tells the truth; voracious wants more.
voracious: Voracious describes a huge appetite or eager consumption. It differs from veracious, which means truthful.
sterilize: Sterilize means eliminate living microorganisms. Disinfect generally means reduce or destroy harmful microorganisms and is not always complete sterilization.
Sterilize is the stronger requirement: no living germs remain.
virulent: Virulent can describe a highly harmful disease agent or intensely bitter hostility. The sentence here uses the hostile figurative sense.
A virulent verbal attack is fiercely malicious.
wan: Wan means pale and weak-looking. It does not mean the same thing as wary, which describes caution.
A wan face has little healthy color.
waive: Waive means voluntarily give up a right or requirement. Wave is the motion of a hand or water.
Waive a fee: choose not to charge it.
xenophobia: Xenophobia is hostility or fear directed toward people perceived as foreign. The word describes prejudice rather than endorsing it.
Xeno- refers to foreign or unfamiliar; -phobia refers to fear.
